It is prevelant among many younger female Americans and you'll find more literature on it there. But I've noticed it among Swedes and Danes when speaking Swedish and Danish.

EDIT: I just found it is a feature in Danish known as "stød", but that's more adding a glottal stop, not creaky voice.

In norwegian the creaky voice thing is called "knirkestemme". I remember having read an article about the advent of "knirkestemme" in norwegian on NRK's website (norway's public broadcasting company, akin to the BBC in britain or the ARD in germany). Here it is: http://www.nrk.no/kultur/stemmeknirk-er-utbredt-1.11554837 google translate will be your friend. They don't cite any studies, but at least they talked to a (norwegian) linguist.

About news anchors that don't creak: they usually talk very clear (clear as in easily understandable). So maybe there's some bias, if creaky voice is seen as compromising clarity in those circles. But outside of news I have heard creaking voices in norwegian media. I don't remember names, though - I don't watch TV or listen to radio very much.

As for location: I don't move around much in Norway so I can only account for the area where I live (the north). I'd say that it's younger people who do it the most, and my gutfeel is that girls do it more often than boys. Overall I don't hear it very often, though - no comparison to american trash tv, at least. I work at a university, and some but not too many of the students I know do it sometimes.
